evidence: CDIAL 6954 explicitly places Dameli nawâsa among early loans from Persian (compare newāse), alongside Kati nəvås, Gawarbati nawāsa and Khowar nəvεs. The Sanskrit nápāt heading and the inherited Ashkun nawā, Waigali nãvā, Kati nəvɔ set are separate from this s-containing loan group. Propose a Persian loan for the masculine and a corresponding feminine formation; immediate historical donor attestation/node still needs resolution. Do not label the Kati parallel a demonstrated Nuristani-to-Dameli loan.

evidence: Perder p. 88 explicitly calls sawa hundred a Pashto loan. Existing Pashto sal/sol hundred does not by itself establish the exact borrowed allomorph sawa. Identify the appropriate donor form before assigning. Existing Table 26 record is already linked in the compiled graph; the prose attestation remains unresolved.

evidence: Perder reports Morgenstierne’s a’zâr four hundred, ultimately Persian hazār thousand, but says his informants did not recognise it and questions the older numeral system. Neither a modern thousand edge nor a confident four-hundred reconstruction is justified.

forms.Source: perder2013dameli[p. 172, example (141), w2, y 375, data TW3007]

evidence: Perder explicitly gives de as the suppletive father stem used with second/third-person kinship suffixes: dēn your father, dēs his/her father, versus unmarked dadi. This establishes membership in the same paradigm, not descent of de from dadi. Overlay accepts neither a suppletive-paradigm relation nor variant assignments; do not mislabel ordinary inflection as derived or inherited reflex of dadi’s etymon.

CDIAL 3489 expressly distinguishes Dameli kučāy scratch oneself from *kōcc thrust/pierce/dig, despite nearby Waigali/Kati kuč dig. Modern kuc scratch should not be attached to the dig etymon on spelling alone. Compare Kalasha kučh scratch, Khowar kučēi and Gawarbati kuča; deeper etymon remains unresolved.

evidence: Perder Table 25 explicitly derives gevanbaṣ able to walk from gew/gev walk with abilitative -baṣ. One compiled derivative already points to the unlinked walk base. This is good synchronic morphology, but the remaining duplicate cannot receive a save-ready ancestry until the base is resolved; do not use that derivative’s blank status to fabricate a supported root.

Perder Table 31 pairs akaṭ come together with first causative akaṭāi mix/put together. The causative relation is explicit; the simple root’s history remains unresolved. Existing derived and variant edges end at unlinked bases, so they do not establish ancestry. Infinitive akaṭan has a combined source gloss that requires checking which valency is intended.

Table 17 labels bawi son-in-law but codes it SW (son’s wife), whereas zamaa carries DH, the expected daughter’s-husband code. This conflicts internally; do not propose an etymology using the masculine gloss before source reconciliation.

Perder example 38 analyses nikʰaa-aw-aai-uma as a second causative exit form, while Table 32 gives nikʰaalawaai from nikʰaal take out. The latter base has an approved CDIAL 7484 analysis. The missing l in example 38 needs explaining before linking this token as an ordinary second causative of nikʰāl.

Possible Nuristani connection/borrowing: compare Kati pr̆uśt, Waigali prōśt and Ashkun prust bed, grouped under the existing Proto-Nuristani *prost node. Perder Table 12 explicitly analyses proś as the reduced standalone form of prośt, restored in prośta in bed. Halfmann p. 54 compares the Nuristani bed family with *prau̯štHa-. These facts support the lexical family but do not identify a historical donor or distinguish borrowing from inheritance; no accepted borrowing edge is proposed.
source_access: Strand compiled/cached comparisons inspected; live Strand URL was unavailable. Halfmann primary PDF and Perder cached grammar read.

evidence: Perder footnote 60 tentatively decomposes agarka if into Urdu agar plus Pashto ka if, or an unidentified Urdu element. The second component and route are unresolved; neither a definite compound nor a direct Sanskrit etymon is justified.

forms.Source: perder2013dameli[p. 156, example (115), w3, y 480, data TW2019]

evidence: Perder says laka like is borrowed and widespread, particularly in Pashto, but this does not identify a unique donor route. Record the areal comparison without promoting it to a demonstrated Pashto loan.

forms.Source: perder2013dameli[p. 125, Table 39, cell 1, y 539];perder2013dameli[p. 77, example (17), w4, y 54];perder2013dameli[p. 173, example (143), w4, y 171, data E0104]

evidence: Perder gives English missed call and telephone as sources in the discussion of conjunct verbs, but p. 9 states English loans reach Dameli through Urdu or Pashto. The ultimate English identification is clear; the immediate transmitting language remains unresolved, so a direct English edge would overstate the evidence.

Perder cautiously suggests that giāċ bring may historically combine gi having brought with āċ come. The proposed first component is not independently resolved and the mapping to the table’s giāg requires its source-form/paradigm check; do not create a confident compound edge from this tentative discussion.

Regional comparison: Dameli inḍorī mortar closely resembles Khowar aṇḍor and Gawarbati hīndūrīk, all independently elicited in Decker’s survey. This supports a shared regional lexical family; the unlinked comparisons do not establish common inheritance or a borrowing direction. Sanskrit ulūkhala and Proto-Nuristani *vāṇ are semantically comparable but lack a demonstrated sound derivation to this form.
citations: decker1992[chitral, locations DML, KIS, GWB, item 31]

evidence: A possible expressive swelling comparison is the CDIAL 9066 phalph family: Oriya phāmpibā swell, Bengali phā̃p swelling, Hindi phā̃pnā swell. This does not supply a demonstrated route to Dameli pʰam: the final m versus nasal-plus-p and the history of the family require evidence. Retain as a lead only, not a reflex assignment.

The meanings cover/hide invite comparison with *tōpyatē (5971) and *stōpyatē (13723), but those entries do not attest Dameli or explain its retroflex initial. The similar *ṭupp branch of CDIAL 5444 means drip and must not be used. The semantic comparison is plausible; ancestry remains unresolved.

The exact-looking Nuristani drāṣ/drās comparisons in CDIAL 6628 mean grape and belong to drākṣā, while Dameli drāṣ here is the verb comb. This is a semantic false match. The scratch/comb searches did not establish an alternative parent; leave unresolved.

Older Dameli truida day after tomorrow supplies a direct lexical comparison for the first word, but the modern record includes postposition ki. A whole-phrase reflex would omit that second component. The ki ancestry is unresolved, so retain the phrase for component analysis rather than silently trimming it.

The Perder record daś hand; ten conflates two homonymous lexical meanings. Both ten and hand have separate established etymological families; assigning the combined record to either one would obscure the other. Source-level separation is needed before a rank-1 ancestry can be accepted.

The kinship qualifiers mažuma/mažumi middle invite comparison with the madhyamá family: Ashkun mā̆zuma, Kati mažime and Pashai manǰumā the middle brother. The kinship heads are transparent, but the qualifier is not independently attested as a Dameli node and the history may involve Nuristani contact. Preserve the comparison and the -ima extension discussed by Turner; do not presume direct descent or a particular Nuristani donor.

The response dēr iśtrī is glossed husband’s sister, but its attested lexical parts mean husband’s brother + wife. A separate response with the same form is correctly compositional for husband’s brother’s wife and is pending in batch 23. This conflicting gloss needs source reconciliation; do not merge the records.

forms.Gloss: a woman who has a car
a woman who has a car

evidence: Perder p. 87 footnote 38 explicitly accepts both gāḍivēla žami and gāḍivēli žami woman who has a car, documenting variable gender agreement. The adjective’s structure is now in batch 24, but the standalone car node and wife/woman base ancestry remain unresolved; no partial phrase ancestry saved.

Perder explicitly analyses this as juxtaposed fields and plots, not one inherited stem. Neither lexical constituent has been resolved to a usable independent Dameli base here; preserve the two-word analysis without inventing an etymon.

Perder explicitly segments aan-o baraan inside and outside, with postpositive coordinator -o. The inside base has accepted ancestry, but barān outside remains unlinked. Do not use a partial component link to imply the whole phrase is etymologised.

Perder gives stone plus wooden beam joined by -o. The stone base bāṭ has reviewed ancestry; an independent Dameli kʰaṭ wooden-beam node is unresolved. The phrase cannot be assigned wholesale to the stone etymon.

Perder gives maize plus wheat joined by -o. The maize term invites comparison with CDIAL10437 yavākāra: Shumasti žuār millet, Hindi jawārā maize, alongside inherited grain terms. Crop-name transfer and immediate borrowing versus inheritance remain unresolved for Dameli žuvār; do not assert this comparison as an accepted component ancestry.

Perder explicitly gives good plus bad joined by -o. The bad base kʰaca has reviewed ancestry, while independently attested abut good remains unlinked. No whole-phrase or one-sided component assignment proposed.

Decker avḍā thirsty matches older Dameli and Savi auḍā thirst. CDIAL495 records a comparison with *apr̥ta unfilled and Morgenstierne’s apūrti, but explicitly observes that neither explains retroflex ḍ. Preserve the primary-source objection; no secure ancestry proposed.

Decker gā speak invites comparison with Dameli gan say, which Turner explicitly places under gaṇáyati. However, the survey form lacks n, and the grammar’s attested say forms retain gan-. Perder also attests homographic gaa as the perfective of go (Appendix 2), so spelling similarity alone cannot decide the analysis. No new inherited or derived link until the survey form is reconciled.

The castration verb śām merits comparison with the ritual slaughter family, not an unqualified link to śamáyati allays. CDIAL12306 distinguishes √śam cut up/prepare a victim and cites Waigali šāmä-istä butchered; the head is the participle śamitá, with śamāyátē and other verbal formations in its prose. This is a possible Nuristani connection, but Dameli’s castrate sense, the exact historical verbal formation, and contact direction are unresolved. Do not attach the bare verb to a similarly spelled participle just to obtain an existing node.

Dameli bait fold and buṭ braid invite comparison with the vartáyati family, under which Turner explicitly records older Dameli baṭyāy wrap. Kashmiri waṭun fold/roll, Bhalessa baṭṭnū fold/roll cloth, and Sindhi vaṭaṇu twist/plait supply close semantic comparisons. The modern forms cannot yet be equated with that older root: bait has a different dental/retroflex sequence and buṭ a different vowel. Preserve the common research lead without merging the two verbs or asserting regular sound changes not established by the sources.

The grammar attests infinitive pɻeyen and root pɻei squeeze. The regional pīḍáyati family has Khowar peḷik wring/squeeze and Punjabi pīṛṇā press, but that comparison does not explain the Dameli initial cluster or establish the required metathesis. Record as a comparative lead only; do not infer a reflex from gloss similarity.

The bury sense invites comparison with *draṭ/*draṭṭ press: Turner cites Sindhi ḍ̠aṭaṇu bury/cork and Gujarati dāṭvũ/ḍāṭvũ bury. Dameli raṭ would require an independently justified change of initial dr- to r-, and its single retroflex does not by itself determine the branch. No assignment proposed; this is a formally incomplete lead.

Dameli prambal light (intransitive) can be compared semantically with prajvalati begin to burn, including Kashmiri pazạlun shine and Hindi pajalnā catch fire. The distinctive Dameli -mb- has not been explained by that comparison, so a prajvalati reflex is not proposed. Its initial pra- is not sufficient evidence for segmentation into a productive modern prefix.

evidence: Modern le/lē much, many, very matches the older Dameli läya mentioned under CDIAL9193 bahura. That mention is a warning rather than a secure etymology: Turner notes that l-initial forms are ambiguous and that Dameli may have original l-, contrasting with proposed bahura developments elsewhere. Preserve Gawarbati lāu/lou and Pashai lau/lāgo as comparisons without assigning Dameli to bahura on the strength of its placement in the entry.

forms.Source: perder2013dameli[p. 132, example (78), w2, y 113, data TW2102];perder2013dameli[p. 131, prose, y 529, x 233, data Q1001]

evidence: Perder explicitly suggests, with uncertainty, ta of plus the conjunctive participle prei having given as the origin of taprei for/on behalf of/because of. The give component has reviewed ancestry but ta of has no established grammaticalisation source (Perder section12.2.1). Preserve the proposed two-component history without inventing ancestry for ta or saving a one-sided component link.

The ingested form mā̃-Ø is glossed his, her, its, but Perder’s possessive paradigm gives mā̃ as first-person singular my, contrasting with sā̃ and third-person forms. This is a gloss/person mismatch requiring source reconciliation before adding ancestry. An independently attested mā̃ my already has a reviewed link; do not treat the mismatched gloss as a new third-person etymon.

forms.Gloss: light up, look good, start to burn

evidence: This additional prambal attestation gives the broader meanings light up, look good, start to burn. It belongs with the previously examined light verb, whose prajvalati comparison leaves -mb- unexplained. Its explicit causative is documented in batch29.

forms.Source: perder2013dameli[p. 177, example (151), w3, y 138, data T3003]

evidence: Perder example151 actually prints daaš stone within baloo daaš, the quoted name of a rock, alongside ordinary baaṭ stone. This is not a secure match to daś hand or daś ten. Preserve the source’s rock-name context; no ancestry or source correction is justified merely by the spelling overlap.

The narrative explicitly contrasts kʰušaali joy with grief, whereas Table22 gives feminine kʰušali intelligent. The long vowel and nominal meaning should not be erased by normalisation. A loan analysis needs its own immediate-donor evidence; the already reviewed adjective is not independent proof for this noun.

evidence: Liljegren and Svärd suggest Dameli-to-Palula transfer of ba, with a possible Waigali be connection. They find no secure deeper etymology. Record possible Nuristani influence without assigning a donor or conflating ba with the copula.

evidence: Dameli zātak child and its regular plural resemble OIA jātaka newborn son (CDIAL5182). But Morgenstierne’s Iranian Elements in Khowar, p671 n1, compares Gawarbati zātak with Middle Persian zātak. This creates a serious regional loan alternative; the citation does not identify a Dameli donor. Preserve inheritance versus borrowing as unresolved.

The tomato response bāṭīŋgar and eggplant response bātīŋgaṛ mūm belong to the regional vātiṅgaṇa comparison. Turner explicitly routes Palula bētiṅgala and Shina bhatiṅgar through Iranian (Persian badiṅgān), rather than direct inherited reflexes. Those comparanda support a loan-family lead for Dameli but do not identify its immediate donor; retain the crop-meaning difference and the unexplained mūm modifier in the eggplant phrase.

Perder p. 41 Table 10 explicitly gives English lamp as the source of lemp lamp. Existing English lamp f_76ko65ts3oqb6 is available, but this statement identifies English origin without ruling out Urdu or Pashto transmission, which Perder discusses generally on p. 9. Hold the immediate borrowed edge until that distinction is resolved; do not silently treat the ultimate English etymon as the immediate donor.

Perder p.109 examples50–51 explicitly gloss aaċ-u-num and aaċ-e-na as take and translate I take / he takes. Elsewhere aaċ is arrive/reach, with aaɡ future (p.98 table28), and CDIAL1044 compares older Dameli āċ come with Nuristani coming verbs. The repeated take gloss may be a source error or a distinct usage, but neither is established. Preserve these two attestations and exclude from automatic grouping under the already reviewed come verb until the semantic discrepancy is resolved.

The separately transcribed bǣt after in Perder p81 example25 may belong with bāt/bat after and the regional baʿd/bād loan family (batch037), but the front-vowel transcription is not yet explained. Preserve its distinct record and exclude it from automatic loan grouping; the final devoicing comparison does not explain this vowel.

forms.Source: perder2013dameli[p. 189, example (168), w1, y 259, data TW7020];perder2013dameli[p. 189, example (168), w3, y 259, data TW7020]

evidence: Dameli barān outside has regional comparanda in the bahira/bāhira outside family: CDIAL9226 Pashai bārə, Gawri bārū and Dumaki bār/barēni, alongside CDIAL9184 Gawarbati berā̃t outside under *bahirānta. Perder p189 example168 attests barān in an echo pair. These comparisons motivate further investigation but do not establish whether Dameli final -ān reflects a suffix or a larger inherited compound, nor distinguish inheritance from borrowing. Do not select 9226 or 9184 simply from shared outside semantics.

Perder identifies śãũ as a true/pure colour intensifier, specifically with blue (Table44 p163), also Table40 p135. The two glosses describe the same attested use. Comparison with CDIAL13112 satya (Gawri sΛčə, Torwali saǰ, Hindi sā̃cā) does not yet explain the absent medial affricate or Dameli initial ś; comparison with CDIAL12520 śuddha (Punjabi suddhā, Hindi sūdhā, Sinhala sudu) leaves consonant loss and vowel/nasality unexplained. No regular sound history or immediate donor established; these are alternatives examined, not proposed ancestry.

evidence: Perder repeatedly attests lāk weep/cry and transparent inflections in -āl, -em, -i-num, -i-nap and conjunctive -i; these establish a single lexical family but not its ancestry. The corpus lead Marathi laḍṇẽ weep belongs to CDIAL10590 raṭati cries/yells alongside Gujarati raṛvũ and Konkani raḍtā. It is not sufficient evidence for Dameli: neither the initial-liquid history nor the k correspondence is established. No attested Nuristani donor or defensible historical parent found in the inspected sources; retain the grouped paradigm for further research rather than forcing the superficially similar Marathi comparison.

Perder distinguishes bay elder brother from general brā brother. Turner9661 explicitly attests Dameli brâ and supplies comparable reduced forms including Kalasha child-language bāya, Punjabi bhāī and various age-specific kin terms. That establishes a relevant comparison but not whether Dameli bay is an inherited expressive variant or a borrowed address term. Do not silently merge with the unrelated bay happen/be able verb.

Perder identifies bibi as elder sister. Platts bībī includes lady, wife and endearment, with bībī jī husband’s sister, but not this exact older-sister relation. A regional honorific loan is possible, as is convergence in an expressive kin term; immediate donor, vowel adaptation and semantic specialization remain unresolved. Do not assign the source gloss wife or a direct Persian ancestry solely from its familiar spelling.

Perder Table17 and both kinship diagrams consistently distinguish kaṛvāsa great-grandson and kaṛvāsi great-granddaughter from navāsa/navāsi grandchildren. The matching ending suggests a possible analogical kinship pattern, but the initial kaṛ- has not been explained or established as a productive prefix. Do not manufacture a kaṛ component or simply assign the full forms to the ancestry of navāsa; the male/female pair can be grouped for further research without asserting historical derivation.

Perder p69 note32 explains dram as a ritually established bond involving shared goat kidneys, preserving a specific blood-brother sense rather than generic friend. CDIAL6753 dhárma supplies a phonologically suggestive dhrama spelling in Ashokan material and religious-duty semantics, but does not attest Dameli or the blood-brother meaning. The ritual context alone cannot establish this etymology: metathesis, semantic specialization and possible loan transmission remain to be demonstrated. Retain dharma only as an unconfirmed research lead.

forms.Source: perder2013dameli[p. 119, example (60), w4, y 237, data E0003];perder2013dameli[p. 215, Appendix 2, y 155, w6];perder2013dameli[p. 216, Appendix 2, y 85, w2]

evidence: Perder Table23 classifies kʰośan happy as invariable, with further text attestations. Regional Persian-origin xuš/khush is a plausible comparison, but it does not explain the entire Dameli form: final -an and aspirated kʰ require evidence. The discussion of borrowed -i adjectives nearby specifically illustrates axiri and does not identify kʰośan’s donor or morphology. Retain as an unresolved contact lead rather than inventing a native -an derivation or dropping that material from the analysis.

forms.Source: perder2013dameli[p. 32, Table 7, cell 1, y 208];perder2013dameli[p. 83, example (29), w5, y 514]

evidence: The survey gūrūm and Perder gurum attest morning; Perder also explicitly identifies gurma ki in the morning as an alternative expression for tomorrow. This supports grouping the morning base and its temporal phrase, but not an inherited etymon. The final -m and vowel pattern need historical explanation. No direct morning etymology for this Dameli form was found in the inspected Turner entries; resemblance to a heat/day word alone would not establish the required semantic and sound history. The phrase is not a simplex tomorrow root.

Dameli mākām is glossed afternoon in the Decker survey. Pashto makham evening is independently attested in thePashto dictionary greeting and a linguistic study of temporal ta, making contact a plausible lead. However, both medial k versus kh and the afternoon/evening distinction require verification; do not silently amend the Dameli source gloss or assert the donor without checking the elicitation and dialect form.

Perder’s wedding narrative explicitly has digar-a afternoon-LOC. Persian/Hindustani digar/dīgar is a relevant formal lead, but the inspected Platts entry supplies other/again, not this temporal sense. The wider prayer-time comparison needs its own primary lexical evidence and transmission argument. Preserve the source afternoon meaning and ordinary locative -a; no assignment to other or to a remote second numeral is justified by this check.

Perder Table39 supplies pui b become = understand, without a standalone gloss for pui. OPED12538 gives Pashto pohedəl understand and its periphrastic preterite poh šu, supporting a possible contact comparison involving a become construction. However, pui versus poh and the precise borrowed unit are unresolved; the entire Pashto verb should not be used as the donor of the Dameli complement. Preserve the blank lexical gloss and record understand only as the whole construction’s meaning.

Perder Table39 gives milau meeting with b become, meaning meet. CDIAL10133 section1 already attests Dameli mili together with in the milati family, so native related vocabulary must be considered alongside borrowing. Platts milāp meeting tentatively equates that word with milāw/milāʾo; the Kalasha dictionary also supplies miláw hik happen/occur. These are useful regional comparanda, but do not settle the Dameli -au formation or loan direction. Do not derive milau automatically from the postposition mili, or assign it to Sanskrit milana merely because both are glossed meeting.

Perder deliberately uses perẽĩ fairy/djinn as an example of the nasal diphthong ẽĩ in Table6, so that ending must be explained rather than normalized away. Platts Persian-origin parī fairy, with associated spirit-possession vocabulary, is a plausible regional comparison; compiled Khowar parí supplies another contact lead. Neither comparison explains the complete Dameli vowel sequence or establishes an immediate donor. Retain this as a possible Persian-family borrowing for further research, not a direct Persian edge or an invented Dameli suffix.

evidence: Perder section12.1.1 identifies ki as a locative-governing postposition marking spatial targets, recipients and beneficiaries; the five records share that function. CDIAL2814’s kr̥tá discussion derives regional Maiya kira and Kohistani Shina kíria for from kr̥té, and CDIAL3428 gives Poguli kica for from kr̥tya. These are functional leads, not exact Dameli attestations: the loss of the medial consonants and the vowel history needed for ki are not established. No direct karoti do edge or automatic homonym merge is justified; retain the whole postposition group for historical research.

evidence: Perder attests ku why independently and tentatively analyses kuitē because as ku plus tē. This establishes the modern base but not its ancestor. CDIAL3166 kím u has interrogative kimu forms and explicitly doubtful direct derivation; CDIAL3271 kútaḥ has Prakrit kuō and Sindhi Kachchhi ko why. Both offer possible histories for a short ku, but neither explicitly attests Dameli or establishes its necessary contraction. Do not choose between them by meaning alone, merge with ku do under karoti, or assume the separately glossed ku or has the same history. The pending kuitē compound therefore remains blocked on its unlinked base.

evidence: Perder’s demonstrative paradigm aligns ayā here with tara there and kā where, confirming a proximal spatial adverb rather than a form of the come verb. CDIAL1605 iha includes Middle Indo-Aryan ia and reinforced iyya, with Western Pahari ia/iyyā; CDIAL228 atra preserves regional tr/t forms. These are alternative deictic leads, but neither establishes the Dameli initial a and the full historical formation. Paradigmatic analogy is possible, not demonstrated. Retain the three attestations together without assigning an unsupported iha or atra ancestry.

Perder Table 6 explicitly documents the nasal diphthong in ṭãũ; Tables 40 and 44 identify ṭãu as the lexicalised intensifier of black and red. It is distinct from pak and śãũ, which intensify other colours. The source establishes function and phonology but supplies no historical derivation. No verified comparative form explaining the retroflex onset and nasal diphthong was found in this pass; do not assign an ancestor merely from the English gloss pure/full.
